{{nihongo|'''Watatsumi Shrine (Kobe)'''|海神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in Miyamoto-chō, {{ill|Tarumi-ku, Kobe|ar|تارومي-كو|ceb|Tarumi Ku|de|Tarumi-ku (Kōbe)|fa|تارومی-کو، کوبه|fr|Tarumi-ku|id|Tarumi-ku, Kobe|it|Tarumi-ku|ja|垂水区|kab|Tarumi-ku|ko|다루미구|ru|Таруми-ку (Кобе)|th|เขตทารูมิ|tr|Tarumi|zh|垂水區|qid=Q1078806}}, {{ill|Kobe|Q48320|qid=Q48320}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|Q130290|qid=Q130290}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}), and under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|Q712534|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|lt=former shrine rank}} it was a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kanpei Chūsha}}. Today, it is listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|Q10898274|qid=Q10898274}} of the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}}. Together with {{ill|Iwa Shrine (Matsumoto)|Q65320|qid=Q65320}} and {{ill|Iibo Nimasu Amaterasu Shrine|Q11604472|qid=Q11604472}}, it is considered one of the Three Great Shrines of {{ill|Harima|Q3783364|qid=Q3783364}}. {{nihongo|'''Watatsumi Shrine (Kobe)'''|海神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Harima Province]].

== Overview ==
In notifications under the Religious Corporations Act, the shrine is read as “Watatsumi Jinja,” but the reading “Kaijinja” is also widely known among local residents and parishioners<ref>{{Cite web |title=How do you read Kobe’s “Watatsumi Shrine”? “Kai,” “Ama,” “Watatsumi”… |url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/odekake-plus/news/detail.shtml?url=news/odekake-plus/news/pickup/201712/10819940 |website=Kobe Shimbun NEXT |date=2017-12-14 |access-date=2025-07-03 |language=Japanese}}</ref><ref>{{National Diet Library Digital Collection|766190/1/21|Sanyō Railway Passenger Guide: also called Illustrated Guide to Famous Places along the Sanyō Road|format=EXTERNAL}}</ref>. In ancient times it was called Amajinja or Tarumijinja, as well as Hyūga Daimyōjin and Izaida Daimyōjin. The reading “Watatsumi” was adopted in Meiji 4 (1871) based on the theory of {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|Q384647|qid=Q384647}}. The *History of Watatsumi Shrine, a Kanpei Chūsha of Harima Province* states that “according to ancient precedent, it should be read Ama or Tarumi.” The reading “Tarumi” derives from the fact that the original name of the enshrined deity was Tarumi-no-Kami. “Ama” comes from the shrine having been the {{ill|Ujigami|Q767655|qid=Q767655}} (clan tutelary deity) of the Ama no Atai (sea-faring clan).

== Enshrined Deities ==
As the three seats of {{ill|Watatsumi|Q1474187|qid=Q1474187|lt=sea deities}}, the following three deities are enshrined as the principal deities, with {{ill|Amaterasu|Q455602|qid=Q455602|lt=Ōhirume no Muchi no Mikoto}} enshrined as an associated deity.
* Uwatsuwatatsumi-no-Kami: deity of the sea surface = navigation
* Nakatsuwatatsumi-no-Kami: deity of the sea depths = fish (fishing)
* Sokotsuwatatsumi-no-Kami: deity of the sea bottom = seaweed and salt

== History ==
According to shrine tradition, when {{ill|Empress Jingū|Q232803|qid=Q232803}} was returning from the {{ill|Three Han Campaign|Q11249435|qid=Q11249435}}, a violent storm arose at sea near this area and her ship was unable to proceed. When the Empress enshrined the three Watatsumi deities, the storm subsided, and in gratitude a shrine building was erected here to enshrine them.

This account closely resembles the foundation legends recorded in the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935}} for {{ill|Hirota Shrine (Osaka City)|Q1466105|qid=Q1466105|lt=Hirota Shrine}}, {{ill|Ikuta Shrine|Q710086|qid=Q710086}}, {{ill|Nagata Shrine|Q661395|qid=Q661395}}, and {{ill|Sumiyoshi-taisha|Q705949|qid=Q705949}}, although the relevant passage in the *Nihon Shoki* does not mention Watatsumi Shrine.

The earliest appearance in documents is in the *{{ill|Shinshō Kyakuchokufushō|Q11502312|qid=Q11502312}}*, dated to Daidō 1 (806), which records the donation of ten {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shinpu}} to Tarumi-no-Kami of Akashi in Harima Province.
Because this site was a key point for maritime transportation, it was revered from early times as a deity protecting sea travel.
In the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}, it is listed as “Watatsumi Shrine, three seats, Akashi District, Harima Province,” and ranked as a Myōjin Taisha.

From the medieval period onward, the shrine declined due to warfare and other factors, but in Tenshō 11 (1587) {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|Q187550|qid=Q187550}} donated mountain forests in Tarumi-gō as prayer offerings. During the Edo period, successive lords of the {{ill|Akashi Domain|Q839406|qid=Q839406}} revered the shrine deeply, making annual visits each February a customary practice.

From the early Edo period it was called “Hyūga Daimyōjin”<ref name="banshu">{{Cite book|Japanese|doi=10.11501/2563455|title=Banshū Meisho Junran Zue, Vol. 2|date=1804|chapterurl={{NDLDC|2563455/24}}|chapter=Tarumi Shrine, Hyūga Myōjin}}</ref>, but when it was ranked as a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kokuhei Chūsha}} in Meiji 4 (1871), it reverted to the name “Watatsumi Shrine.” In Meiji 30 (1897), it was promoted to Kanpei Chūsha.

Until before the period of high economic growth, the area around the great torii gate was a sandy beach, making it literally a “shrine of the sea”<ref name="banshu" />. However, from 1960 onward land reclamation was carried out, and the area in front of the great torii became roads and a fishing port<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese|url=https://www.kobe-np.co.jp/news/kobe/202201/0014966735.shtml |title=Tarumi once had sandy beaches, Maiko had only a few pine trees—why did the scenery change? |publisher=Kobe Shimbun NEXT |date=2022-01-07 |accessdate=2022-01-07}}</ref>.

== Rituals ==
== Ebisu Festival ==
As at {{ill|Nishinomiya Shrine|Q705297|qid=Q705297}}, {{ill|Ebisu (mythology)|Q1129330|qid=Q1129330}} is also a sea deity, so the festival is held for three days around {{ill|January 10|Q2243|qid=Q2243}} each year.

; {{ill|Sacred Sites of Kamigata|ja|神仏霊場巡拝の道|zh|神佛靈場巡拜之道|qid=Q10444949}}

== Other ==
Until {{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}} 18 (2006), a fireworks display dedicated to the shrine was held every {{ill|July|Q121|qid=Q121}} during the summer festival, but from the following year onward, while the summer festival continued as before, the fireworks display was discontinued. {{Citation needed|date=January 2012|The {{ill|Akashi pedestrian bridge accident|Q4700349|qid=Q4700349}} that occurred in Heisei 13 (2001) is believed to have had no small influence.}}
